Q1_text: Three or four. A pipeline health board in Grafana, the freshness dashboard from our dbt runs, an incident board, and then the product usage dashboard which the PM team also uses. On the freshness one the first thing I look at is the list of models that have breached their SLA overnight. On the product one I look at the event volume by platform before I look at any metric, because a metric built on half the events is worse than no metric.
Q2_text: A few weeks ago we had to decide whether to roll back a release because activation rate looked like it had dropped about 9 per cent. The dashboard was clear, there was a step change on the release date. What I noticed first was that the drop was only on iOS and only for new installs. Before deciding I checked the raw event counts and the app version distribution, and it turned out the SDK on the new build was batching events differently so a chunk of them were arriving after our daily cut off. The activation was fine, the counting was late. We did not roll back, we changed the cut off. It took about three hours to establish that, and in those three hours there was quite a lot of pressure to just roll back.
Q3_text: In our own stack, yes, quite well, because we set it up deliberately. Every table has a freshness test and the dashboard shows a stale badge if the last successful run is outside the window. Downstream tiles grey out. That said, I want to be careful here, because the badge only covers the failures we anticipated. A pipeline that runs successfully with a partial payload from an upstream API is still green, and we have been caught by exactly that. So the warning tells me when the plumbing broke, not when the data is wrong. Those are different problems and only one of them is solved.
Q4_text: Yes. Our churn model dashboard once showed a very healthy retention curve for a cohort that I knew, from talking to two customer success people, was in a bad state. Two of those accounts had already told their CSM they were evaluating alternatives. The dashboard did not know anything about that because it only sees product events, and both of those customers had actually increased usage while running an evaluation of the competitor. So the signal was real, the interpretation was completely wrong. Usage went up because they were doing a migration assessment.
Q5_text: I raised it in our weekly business review and wrote it up in the analytics channel with the specific account IDs. It was received well and we added a manual override field so CSMs can flag an account regardless of what the model says. So in this case it did go somewhere, and it is recorded in the sense that there is a Slack thread and a Linear ticket. But I would not call that a record in the way you mean. In six months nobody will find that thread. There is no register of times the model was wrong, which is a bit ironic for a data team.
Q6_text: Here it is a mixed picture and I think we are better than most. In postmortems we genuinely operate blameless and a well argued judgement call is accepted if you wrote down your reasoning at the time. The written reasoning is the key. If you decided something in your head and it went wrong, that is hard to defend. If there is a doc with your reasoning dated before the outcome, you are fine even if you were wrong. So it is not report versus judgement exactly, it is documented versus undocumented.
Q7_text: For me personally the two are fairly similar, and I know that is not the common answer. Our engineering culture treats an outage the same way whether the dashboard was followed or not, the question is what did the decision maker know at the time. Having said that, I have worked in two other companies where it was not like this at all, and there overruling was career limiting. So I would say my answer is about my current employer and not about the industry.
Q8_text: Frequently. Our support engineers see the same three complaints in tickets long before it shows up in any metric. There is a channel where they post it. Whether it is recorded depends entirely on whether someone converts it to a ticket, and that in turn depends on how busy that week is. I would guess more than half of it evaporates. We tried tagging tickets by theme but the tagging is done by the person closing the ticket, who wants to close the ticket.
Q9_text: It narrows things but in a specific way. The dashboard makes incremental options very easy to discuss, because you can see the metric moving. Anything structural is hard to discuss because there is no tile for it. For example, deprecating a feature that a small number of large accounts use is almost never proposed, because the dashboard shows usage but not the strategic cost of keeping it. So we end up optimising the things that are measured and quietly not deciding the things that are not.
Q10_prompt: In the study you have just completed, in the scenario about renewing a supplier at increased volume the dashboard indicated that the supplier scored 98.6 per cent and should be renewed at higher volume, while what you knew locally was that the inspector had been passing batches by eye because the test rig was out of calibration. You chose: Renew at the current volume rather than increasing it.Looking back, what would drive your choice if this were a real decision at your work?
Q10_text: I picked the middle option there, renew at the current volume, and that is very typical of me. Reading it back, I think the middle option is a way of not making the decision. It looks prudent but it leaves the underlying question, is the measurement trustworthy, completely unanswered, and you carry that unanswered question forward at a lower volume. What would drive me in a real situation is whether the measurement failure is recoverable quickly. If recalibrating the rig takes two days, hold, obviously. If it takes six weeks, then the middle option is genuinely reasonable and you manage the risk with incoming inspection. I did not think about that at the time. I think I chose the middle option because it felt safe rather than because I had a view.
Q11_text: Show the provenance of the number where the number is, and make it socially normal to ask. In my team we have a running joke that the first question in any review is what is the denominator, and because it is a joke it is safe to ask. That is more useful than any tooling we have built. If you want people to push back you have to make the pushback low cost and slightly boring, not brave.
Q12_text: Nothing further, other than to say the scenarios were well constructed. The one about the vibration sensor reading the same value every time was a nice touch, that is a real failure mode and it is very hard to see on a chart.

What I noticed was that the attribution model gives last click credit and this channel was mostly retargeting, so it was taking credit for users who were coming anyway. I ran a simple holdout comparison for two weeks. The incremental effect was much smaller than the dashboard suggested. Q3_text: For my own tables I know, because I wrote freshness checks and they post to a channel if a load is late. For the tables I did not build, I have no idea, and some of them are pulled from a third party connector that fails silently maybe once a fortnight. When it fails the dashboard does not go blank, it just shows a lower number for that day, and the marketing team reads it as a bad day. I have explained this several times.
Q4_text: Yes. A dashboard showed our email open rate jumping to something like 68 per cent which is not realistic for our list. It was the Apple privacy change causing automatic opens to register. So the data was accurate and the metric had become meaningless, which is a different problem from a broken feed but it has the same effect on decisions.
Q5_text: I wrote it up in a short doc and shared it with the marketing team and my manager. The response was that we should keep tracking it since we have historical data for it. Which is exactly the wrong reason. It was not recorded as a caveat on the dashboard itself, so anyone opening that dashboard today still sees the same number with no note. I did add a footnote once and it got removed in a redesign.
Q6_text: Whatever is on the dashboard, because that is what everyone has already seen. Once a number has been in a weekly review deck three times it becomes true regardless of how it is calculated. Changing it later is harder than getting it right at the start, because now you are not correcting a number, you are contradicting three months of meetings.
Q7_text: I am an analyst so I am not the decision maker, but there is a version of this for me. If I produce the number and the decision goes wrong, nobody blames the analyst. If I challenge a number and I turn out to be wrong, that is remembered, because I have wasted people's time and created doubt. So the safe thing for an analyst is to deliver the number and mention concerns quietly. I think that is a real bias in how analysts behave and I do not think anyone measures it.
Q8_text: Our customer support lead told us the NPS dashboard was misleading because the survey only goes to users who complete a transaction, so unhappy users who abandon are never surveyed. She said it in a meeting. It is a completely valid point, it is survivorship bias. Nothing was recorded, nothing changed, and the NPS number is still on the leadership dashboard with no caveat. I would say this is the single clearest case I have seen of a correct objection going nowhere.

suspicion_text: How organisations use performance reports for taking operational decisions.
Q1_text: We have a monitoring portal where the field offices upload their progress every month, and there is a dashboard on top of it which the department sees. Apart from that I get an Excel MIS compiled by our section. I open the portal dashboard mainly before the review meeting and the first thing I look at is the physical progress against target for each district, because that is what will be asked in the meeting.
Q2_text: Last year there was a proposal to shift some allocation from one district to another because the portal showed very low utilisation in one district for two quarters. I was asked to put up a note. What I noticed was that the district in question had a vacancy in the post of the officer who does the data entry, which was known to us, and the works were actually going on at site. So the low utilisation was a reporting failure and not a physical failure. I called the district office, got the measurement book entries and the photographs, and put up a note recommending that the reallocation be deferred by one quarter. It was accepted. But I want to say clearly, if I had simply forwarded the dashboard figure the reallocation would have gone through and a working district would have been penalised.
Q3_text: There is a last updated date on the portal but it only tells you when somebody last logged in and saved, not whether the entry is complete or correct. There is no warning of any kind for a district that has not reported. It simply shows zero, and zero looks like poor performance rather than missing data. This is the single biggest problem with the portal and it has been pointed out many times. What makes me doubt a figure is when a district shows exactly the same figure two months running, or when a figure is exactly at the target, because in the field nothing is exactly at target.
Q4_text: Many times. The clearest one was a beneficiary count which showed a very large jump in one month for one block. Not possible physically because the camps had not even been held. On enquiry it was found that the entries of three months had been uploaded together after the connectivity was restored, so all of it landed in one month. The block looked like a star performer that month and like a failure for the three months before.
Q5_text:
I raised it in writing, which in our system is easy, and that is exactly the point I want to make. Here is what happened:
1. I put up a file noting explaining the backlog upload issue.
2. The note was seen by my superior and forwarded to the IT section.
3. The IT section replied that the portal is working as designed.
4. The matter was closed at that.
So it was recorded, properly, with a file number, and it is traceable even today. But recording is not the same as answering. Nobody was required to fix anything, and the same thing happened again in the next monsoon. In our system everything is written and very little is answered. I think that is the opposite of most private companies where nothing is written but somebody at least shouts and it gets fixed.
Q6_text: In government the file is everything. If it is on the file it can be defended, in audit, in an assembly question, anywhere. A decision taken on personal judgement, however correct, is very difficult to defend later, because the person who took it may be transferred and the person answering has only the file. So we all write. The unfortunate effect is that we write to protect rather than to explain, and a file that protects everybody explains nothing.
Q7_text: This I can answer very clearly. If you follow the system, the portal, the guidelines, the sanctioned procedure, and the outcome is bad, nothing happens to you personally. The procedure is blamed. If you deviate, even for a good reason, and the outcome is bad, then it is a personal matter and it may come up in the audit para or in the vigilance angle. That fear is real and it is the main reason officers do not deviate. Even where the guideline is clearly not suited to the local situation, we will follow it and put the difficulty on record, which is a way of protecting yourself without solving the problem.
Q8_text: Constantly. Our block level officers know exactly which figures are unreliable. They mention it in the monthly video conference. The minutes of the video conference are circulated, so technically it is recorded. But minutes in our system are a summary written by the section, and the disagreements do not survive the summarising. Two lines of an officer's objection become the phrase the district was advised to expedite data entry. The objection has been recorded and simultaneously erased.
Q9_text: Yes, considerably. The portal has certain fields, so the review meeting is about those fields, physical progress, financial progress, utilisation certificates. Anything not on the portal cannot be discussed usefully because there is no figure to quote. For instance the quality of the work done, or whether the location chosen is the right one, has no field, so it never comes up in the review even though it matters more than the percentage.
Q10_prompt: In the study you have just completed, in the scenario about choosing where to open the next store the dashboard indicated that the site scored 87 and should be opened next quarter, while what you knew locally was that the footfall counter at that site had been offline for 47 days. You chose: Recommend Tiruppur for Q3, as the Site Score indicates.Looking back, what would drive your choice if this were a real decision at your work?
Q10_text: I recommended the town as per the site score. Reading it back I would defend it in one way and not in another. In our system the site score would be the sanctioned methodology, and if I recommend against the sanctioned methodology on the basis of what one field officer told me verbally, my note will be returned with the query as to what is the basis. Meena's statement is not a basis I can put on a file. So the honest driver is that the file needs a documentary basis and the local knowledge does not have one. What I would do in practice is exactly what I described earlier, I would ask for a two week enumeration so that the local knowledge becomes a document, and then I can act on it. The delay is not caution, it is the time it takes to convert knowledge into a form the file will accept.
Q11_text: Allow the field officer's objection to be entered in the portal itself, against the figure, and require the higher office to record a reply before the report can be closed for that month. Not a committee, not a meeting, just a field that cannot stay empty. In our system anything that blocks the next step gets done, and anything that does not block the next step does not.
Q12_text: You have not asked about transfers. In government the person who raised the concern is often not there six months later, and the person who arrives has no idea it was ever raised. Any solution that depends on a person remembering will fail in our set up. It has to be in the record and it has to be linked to the figure itself.

1. I put up a file noting explaining the backlog upload issue.

Q7_text: This I can answer very clearly. If you follow the system, the portal, the guidelines, the sanctioned procedure, and the outcome is bad, nothing happens to you personally. Whether managers keep following the dashboard even when the brief clearly says the data is not reliable.
Q1_text: Mostly client dashboards, so it changes every project. Currently it is a Power BI supply chain dashboard on the client side and one internal utilisation tracker. When the client dashboard opens I look at the summary KPI row first because that is what goes into the steering committee deck. Internally the first thing is my own utilisation percentage, which decides how my week looks.
Q2_text: On my current project we had to recommend which of two distribution centres should absorb extra volume. The dashboard showed one DC with much better cost per case. I noticed first that the better DC had a smaller product mix, mainly fast movers, so cost per case was not comparable. I flagged it to my manager and we normalised the comparison by product family before it went into the deck. In the end the recommendation changed. But I should be clear, I did not decide anything, I raised it and my manager decided.
Q3_text: Honestly I take the client's data as given. That is more or less the rule on our engagements, we are not there to audit their systems and if we start questioning the source data the timeline goes for a toss. If the client's team says this is the extract, we use it. Whether there is a warning on their dashboards, I do not know, I have not looked for one. The only check we do is a total reconciliation against their finance figures at the start, and after that we assume it holds for the whole project.
Q4_text: There was one instance. A headcount dashboard was showing attrition much lower than what the HR team was telling us in interviews. I mentioned it once in a team meeting. It turned out the dashboard was counting only permanent employees and the client's contract workforce was almost 40 per cent. So it was not wrong, it was just answering a different question than the one we were asking.
Q5_text: I told my manager and he told the client counterpart. It was corrected in the definition of the metric for our analysis. But nothing was written down. There was no note anywhere that the dashboard is misleading for anyone else who uses it. We fixed it for our deck and moved on. I do remember thinking that everyone else in that client organisation is still looking at the same wrong number, but it was not our scope.
Q6_text: Whatever is in the deck. In consulting the deck is the record. If it is a client decision then the deck we submitted is what protects both sides, and that is why the appendix has all the source references. Personal judgement carries weight only from partners. If I as an analyst say something feels off, the response is usually can you show it in the data, and if I cannot show it in the data in the next two hours then it does not exist for practical purposes.
Q7_text: At my level I am not really the one following or overruling, so it is a bit hypothetical. But from what I have seen, if the recommendation came from the analysis and it does not work out, the discussion is about assumptions. If someone had gone against the analysis, then it becomes personal. Also honestly I would never overrule anything, that is not my role. I would raise it and then it becomes my manager's call, which is a comfortable position to be in.
Q8_text: On one project the client's warehouse in charge kept telling us the system stock is never matching physical stock. We noted it in our interview notes. It did go into the report, as a data quality observation in the appendix. Whether anybody read the appendix, I do not know. Nothing was done about it during our engagement. The recommendations were based on the system stock anyway, because that was all we had.
Q9_text: Yes, it does. Whatever the dashboard shows becomes the shape of the analysis and then the shape of the recommendation. On the DC question, everything we discussed was about cost per case, service level and capacity, because that is what the dashboard had. Nobody discussed whether the customer promise itself could be changed, or whether some SKUs should not be stocked at all, because there was no data view for that and building one was not in scope.
Q10_prompt: In the study you have just completed, in the scenario about a delivery route reporting itself as on target the dashboard indicated that the route was at 96 per cent on time and needed no action, while what you knew locally was that the depot supervisor had reported loads arriving without paperwork. You chose: Take no action. The route is green and within service level.Looking back, what would drive your choice if this were a real decision at your work?
Q10_text: I chose to take no action since the route was green. Looking at it now, the supervisor phoning twice is quite a strong signal and I did not weigh it at all. I think in my head green means somebody else has already looked at it. What would drive my choice in a real project is what my manager and the client expect me to produce. If I flag something that is showing green, the immediate question will be do you have data, and I would not have data, only a phone call from a supervisor. Also I would worry about looking like I am creating work. So I would probably mention it verbally and not put it in the deck, which I now realise is the same as doing nothing.
Q11_text: If the person raising the doubt does not have to prove it themselves. Right now the burden is fully on whoever speaks up, and at my level that burden is impossible, so nobody speaks up. Maybe a simple thing on the dashboard where you can mark a number as doubtful and it stays visible to others, so at least it is not lost.
Q12_text: Nothing further really. It made me think about the appendix thing, that we found a problem and left it in an appendix. That was a slightly uncomfortable realisation.

Q1_text: A risk and control dashboard that consolidates the operational loss events, key risk indicators and open audit issues, plus a separate limits monitoring screen. I open the KRI screen daily and the loss event screen weekly. The first thing I look at is not a KPI at all, it is the number of indicators that have not been updated this period. An indicator that has not moved is either a very stable process or a broken feed, and in fifteen years I have found it is usually the second.
Q2_text: We had to decide whether to raise the residual risk rating on a payments process after a set of near misses. The dashboard showed the KRI comfortably within appetite, green, for six consecutive months. What I noticed was that the threshold for that indicator had been recalibrated eleven months earlier and nobody had revisited it after a system migration, so the measure was green against a limit that no longer described the process. I asked for the raw event counts rather than the RAG status, and I asked the process owner to walk me through what the indicator actually counts. It counted rejected payments, not failed reconciliations, which was the exposure we were worried about. We raised the rating and put a specific action on the indicator definition itself.
Q3_text: Partly. Our governance tooling shows an as of date for each indicator and a flag if the submission is overdue, so a missing submission is visible. What is not visible is a submission that arrived on time and is wrong, and that is by far the more common failure. Someone under time pressure at quarter end will submit last quarter's figure rather than show the box as outstanding, because an outstanding box gets escalated and a repeated figure does not. That is a control weakness created by the reporting design itself, and I would say it is present in every institution I have worked in.
Q4_text: Frequently, but the clearest case was a fraud losses figure that showed a marked improvement across two quarters. I did not believe it because the underlying transaction volumes had grown and no control had changed. On investigation, a category of loss was being booked to a different general ledger line following a reorganisation, so it simply left the report. Nothing had improved. The exposure was identical and our reported number was better, which is the worst of both worlds.
Q5_text: I escalated it formally. In our environment there is a defined route, it goes to the operational risk committee with a paper, the business has to respond in writing before the next meeting, and the minutes record both the challenge and the response. So yes, it was written down, and the response was on the record too. Internal audit later picked up the same point and referred to our paper. I would say this is one of the few places I have worked where the challenge genuinely survives contact with the organisation. It survives because it is a regulatory expectation, not because we are virtuous.
Q6_text: Documented evidence carries the weight, but I would qualify that. A report is easy to defend only until somebody competent asks how the report is constructed. In a regulatory examination, a decision defended purely by pointing at a dashboard is weak, because the examiner will ask what assurance you have over the dashboard. So at senior level the reliable defence is a documented rationale that references the data and its limitations. Junior colleagues have not learnt this yet, they think the report is the shield. The report is the shield only if nobody looks behind it.
Q7_text: In my institution the two are closer than in most places, deliberately. If you follow the model and the outcome is poor, you will be asked what challenge you applied, and having applied none is itself a finding. If you overrule the model and the outcome is poor, you will be asked to produce your rationale, and if it is documented and reasonable, that is accepted. So both are answerable, which is what you want. Having said that, I have worked in organisations where following was completely safe and departing was not, and I can tell you the behaviour of the staff in those two environments is entirely different. It is not about the people.
Q8_text: Yes, and this is where I would be less complacent about my own organisation. A branch operations officer raised repeatedly that a particular reconciliation was being signed off without the supporting extract because the extract had not run. She raised it with her line manager. It did not reach the risk function for nearly a year, because the route that exists at committee level does not exist at counter level. When it did surface, in an audit, it was treated seriously. But the formal machinery I described earlier begins somewhere above where the knowledge actually is, and that is the honest gap.

Q1_text:
Four regularly:
- an engineering delivery dashboard, cycle time and deployment frequency
- a service health board, error rates and latency
- a product analytics dashboard for the funnels my teams own
- a hiring and attrition view, weekly
On the delivery one the first thing I look at is the spread, not the average. Median cycle time tells me almost nothing. The p90 tells me where people are stuck, and that is the conversation worth having in a one to one.
Q2_text: We were deciding whether to invest a quarter in reducing build times, which is not a glamorous investment. The dashboard showed average build time around 11 minutes, which does not sound like a crisis. What I noticed was that the average included cached builds, which are almost instant, and the real cold builds were around 40 minutes and were what engineers actually experienced before a release. I asked for the distribution, then I asked three engineers to log what they experienced for a week. The lived number was far worse than the reported one. We funded the work. The interesting part is that the dashboard was not wrong, it was answering a question nobody had asked.
Q3_text: For the service health board, yes, we have monitoring on the monitoring, and if a metrics pipeline stops we get paged, because a silent dashboard during an incident is worse than no dashboard. For the product analytics, only sometimes. For the hiring dashboard, no, and that one is entirely manual, somebody updates a sheet. So my confidence varies enormously across four screens that all look equally authoritative, and that is the thing that worries me. They all have the same visual weight. A hand maintained sheet and an alerted pipeline should not look the same on a wall display, but they do.
Q4_text: Yes. Our incident dashboard showed a big improvement in mean time to recovery over two quarters. I did not believe it because nothing structural had changed, we had not invested in on call tooling, nothing. What had happened was that the definition of incident start had quietly shifted to when the incident channel was created rather than when the first alert fired, and channel creation happens after somebody has already started debugging. So we were measuring from a later starting point and calling it improvement.
Q5_text: I raised it in our engineering leadership review and asked for it to be minuted, which it was, and we wrote a short doc on the metric definition and versioned it. So it was recorded and it was answered, and I think the reason is that I was senior enough to insist. That is the uncomfortable finding for me personally. The mechanism did not catch it, my seniority did. If a staff engineer had raised the same point it would have gone into a thread and died there. We have a formal route and it works well for the people who least need it.
Q6_text: Data wins arguments but does not win decisions. In practice, a decision backed by a report is much easier to defend afterwards, and everybody knows it, so people go and find the report that supports the thing they already wanted. I have watched this happen and I have done it. The honest version of the question is not report versus judgement, it is whether people are allowed to say I do not have data and here is my reasoning. In my org they are allowed to, up to about two levels below me, and then it stops.
Q7_text: On paper the same, in practice not. Our postmortems are genuinely blameless and I would defend that. But there is a second layer. Following the dashboard and being wrong costs you nothing socially. Overruling it and being wrong costs you a small amount of credibility that you spend in the next argument. It is not a formal penalty, nobody writes it down, it is much more like a running account that people keep in their heads. That account is the real accountability system and it does not appear in any policy document.
Q8_text: A support engineer told us for months that a particular error was affecting a small number of customers very badly, and the error rate dashboard showed it as a rounding error, which it was, in percentage terms. Percentage terms was the wrong frame, those customers were three of our largest. It was recorded, in tickets, and the tickets were correctly prioritised by the rules we had written, which is to say deprioritised. Nothing was broken. The system worked exactly as designed and produced the wrong outcome, which I find more troubling than if somebody had simply ignored him.
Q9_text: Yes, and I think this is underrated. The dashboard defines the unit of discussion. Because we measure cycle time per team, all our improvement conversations are about a team's process. Nobody questions the good news, and the good news is where the errors hide.
Q12_text: One methodological point, if it is useful. You are asking people to recall occasions when they doubted a dashboard. Those are memorable. The interesting cases are the ones where the dashboard was wrong and nobody doubted it, and by definition nobody can tell you about those. Whatever you find, the real number is worse.

Q1_text:
Four regularly:
- an engineering delivery dashboard, cycle time and deployment frequency
- a service health board, error rates and latency
- a product analytics dashboard for the funnels my teams own
- a hiring and attrition view, weekly
On the delivery one the first thing I look at is the spread, not the average. Median cycle time tells me almost nothing. The p90 tells me where people are stuck, and that is the conversation worth having in a one to one.
Q2_text: We were deciding whether to invest a quarter in reducing build times, which is not a glamorous investment. The dashboard showed average build time around 11 minutes, which does not sound like a crisis. What I noticed was that the average included cached builds, which are almost instant, and the real cold builds were around 40 minutes and were what engineers actually experienced before a release. I asked for the distribution, then I asked three engineers to log what they experienced for a week. The lived number was far worse than the reported one. We funded the work. The interesting part is that the dashboard was not wrong, it was answering a question nobody had asked.
Q3_text: For the service health board, yes, we have monitoring on the monitoring, and if a metrics pipeline stops we get paged, because a silent dashboard during an incident is worse than no dashboard. For the product analytics, only sometimes. For the hiring dashboard, no, and that one is entirely manual, somebody updates a sheet. So my confidence varies enormously across four screens that all look equally authoritative, and that is the thing that worries me. They all have the same visual weight. A hand maintained sheet and an alerted pipeline should not look the same on a wall display, but they do.
Q4_text: Yes. Our incident dashboard showed a big improvement in mean time to recovery over two quarters. I did not believe it because nothing structural had changed, we had not invested in on call tooling, nothing. What had happened was that the definition of incident start had quietly shifted to when the incident channel was created rather than when the first alert fired, and channel creation happens after somebody has already started debugging. So we were measuring from a later starting point and calling it improvement.
Q5_text: I raised it in our engineering leadership review and asked for it to be minuted, which it was, and we wrote a short doc on the metric definition and versioned it. So it was recorded and it was answered, and I think the reason is that I was senior enough to insist. That is the uncomfortable finding for me personally. The mechanism did not catch it, my seniority did. If a staff engineer had raised the same point it would have gone into a thread and died there. We have a formal route and it works well for the people who least need it.
Q6_text: Data wins arguments but does not win decisions. In practice, a decision backed by a report is much easier to defend afterwards, and everybody knows it, so people go and find the report that supports the thing they already wanted. I have watched this happen and I have done it. The honest version of the question is not report versus judgement, it is whether people are allowed to say I do not have data and here is my reasoning. In my org they are allowed to, up to about two levels below me, and then it stops.
Q7_text: On paper the same, in practice not. Our postmortems are genuinely blameless and I would defend that. But there is a second layer. Following the dashboard and being wrong costs you nothing socially. Overruling it and being wrong costs you a small amount of credibility that you spend in the next argument. It is not a formal penalty, nobody writes it down, it is much more like a running account that people keep in their heads. That account is the real accountability system and it does not appear in any policy document.
Q8_text: A support engineer told us for months that a particular error was affecting a small number of customers very badly, and the error rate dashboard showed it as a rounding error, which it was, in percentage terms. Percentage terms was the wrong frame, those customers were three of our largest. It was recorded, in tickets, and the tickets were correctly prioritised by the rules we had written, which is to say deprioritised. Nothing was broken. The system worked exactly as designed and produced the wrong outcome, which I find more troubling than if somebody had simply ignored him.
Q9_text: Yes, and I think this is underrated. The dashboard defines the unit of discussion. Because we measure cycle time per team, all our improvement conversations are about a team's process. Nothing on any screen represents the cost of coordination between teams, which is where most of our actual delay comes from. So we have spent two years optimising within boxes and the thing between the boxes has never once been on an agenda, because it has no owner and no tile.

I have been thinking about why, because I asked for more checks on every single one of these situations and yet on that one I went with the engine. I think it was because the pricing engine was described in a way that sounded like a specialist system and pricing is not my discipline, so I deferred to the specialist. That is the same mechanism I complain about in others, deferring to a system because it is outside your competence. What would actually drive it in my work is whether I can name the failure mode. Here I can, a crawler that has been failing since June is a stale cache, that is an ordinary engineering failure and I would never accept a number from a cache that old. I did not see it because it was dressed as pricing rather than as data.

Q1_text: A fraud operations monitor showing queue volumes, ageing and closure rates, a rules performance dashboard showing hit rate and false positive rate by rule, and a losses dashboard weekly. On the operations monitor the first thing I look at is intake volume, not the open queue. Open queue is an output. If intake looks odd then everything downstream is meaningless, and that is a lesson we learnt the hard way.
Q2_text: Around eight months back the false positive rate on one rule dropped sharply and the dashboard flagged it as an improvement in rule performance. The team was quite pleased. What I noticed is that the drop coincided with a change window and the alert volume for that rule had also fallen, so the ratio improved because the numerator and denominator had both moved for a reason that had nothing to do with the rule getting better. I asked for the raw alert counts by hour and it was clear that alerts had stopped firing for a segment of transactions after a field mapping change. We got it corrected in about two days. If we had accepted the improvement we would have been blind on that segment for who knows how long.
Q3_text: Reasonably well for my own area, because after that incident we built a simple intake monitor that alerts if hourly volume falls below a floor. That is the only reason I would catch it. The main case management dashboards do not warn you about anything, they just show what is in the table. And I would make one point which I think is important for your study. A fraud queue going quiet looks exactly like success. Every other kind of failure looks like a problem, so somebody investigates. This one looks like a win, so people celebrate it, and that is why it is dangerous.
Q4_text: Yes, the one I just described is the main one. There was another where the confirmed loss figure looked far too low for a month and it turned out that cases pending customer confirmation were excluded, and a backlog in that step had grown, so a large amount of loss was sitting in a status that the report did not count. Not wrong, just invisible.
Q5_text: I raised the intake one in the daily huddle and then formally to my head, and a defect was logged with the technology team. It is recorded to that extent, there is a ticket and it was discussed in the monthly risk forum. But the ticket records the technical fix. What is not recorded anywhere is the period during which our monitoring was blind, and that is the thing a regulator would actually want to know. We remediated the cause and we never quantified the exposure window. I have thought about that several times since.
Q6_text: In our function, a number with a lineage. If you can show the query and the table, the discussion is over. Judgement is respected in this team more than in most, because fraud work involves a lot of pattern recognition that cannot be evidenced immediately, but even here you eventually have to convert the hunch into a query. And yes, a decision backed by a report is much easier to defend, particularly when it is reviewed by people outside the function who only have the report.
Q7_text: Not the same. If I follow the system and there is a loss, it is a control gap and there is a remediation plan. If I overrule the system, say I hold a batch of transactions on a hunch and it causes customer complaints and business impact, then it is my call and I will be asked to justify it in a way that is quite personal. I have done it twice and both times I wrote a mail before acting, timestamped, explaining why. That mail is not required by any process. I write it because I know how the conversation goes afterwards.
Q8_text: Our analysts are the closest to the ground and they notice things weeks before any dashboard. One of them said for about a month that the profile of cases coming through one channel felt different, more test transactions, small amounts. There was no metric for feel. It was mentioned in huddles. Nothing was written. Then a campaign of card testing hit us and afterwards, in the review, several people said that analyst had been saying it all along. He had. It just had nowhere to go. We now have a small observations log in the team, which is entirely because of that episode, and I would say half its entries are noise, but the other half is the earliest warning we have.
Q9_text: Yes. The dashboard frames everything as queue management, so our options are add analysts, change thresholds, or reprioritise. Options that never come up are things like slowing down a customer journey to add friction for a segment, because the cost of that sits with the business and there is no shared screen for it. So we optimise inside our box and the better answer often lives outside it.
Q10_prompt: In the study you have just completed, in the scenario about a fraud review queue that had gone quiet the dashboard indicated that the queue was clear and the ageing indicator was green, while what you knew locally was that two analysts had had almost nothing to review since a weekend release. You chose: Report the improvement. The queue is clear and the indicator is green.Looking back, what would drive your choice if this were a real decision at your work?
Q10_text: That was the very first situation I saw and I chose to report the improvement, which is genuinely embarrassing because it is exactly my job and exactly the failure mode I described to you above. I read it too quickly and I answered the way the screen invited me to answer. What I would like to say is that it proves your point better than a careful answer would. In real life, at my desk, with my own monitor, I would never do it, because I have the intake monitor and I have been burnt. But strip away the tooling I built after being burnt and put me in front of a clean green screen at speed, and I behaved like everyone else. The thing that would drive it in reality is not my knowledge, it is whether there is something on the screen that makes the quiet queue look suspicious rather than successful.
Q11_text: Make the absence of data look like an alert rather than like good news. Any metric where zero is the desirable direction needs a floor as well as a ceiling. If my queue drops below the expected band, that should be red, not green. Technically trivial, and almost nobody does it.
Q12_text: Only that you might look at how quickly people answered your first scenario compared to the last one. Mine would tell a story.

Q1_text: The one I open every morning is the bed occupancy and census report, which comes from the HIS. Along with that there is a daily operations summary which the MIS team sends by mail at 8 am, that is a PDF, and an OT utilisation report weekly. When the occupancy screen opens the first thing I see is the ward wise vacancy position and the discharges expected today, because the whole day's planning depends on those two numbers. After that I look at the ALOS for the previous week.
Q2_text: Recently we had to decide on opening eight additional beds in the medical ward for the season. The dashboard showed occupancy at 84 per cent for the previous month which is below our threshold of 88 for expansion. What I noticed was that our occupancy is calculated at midnight census, and our load is highest between 2 pm and 10 pm, so the midnight figure understates the actual crowding badly. I asked the nursing superintendent for the afternoon census of the same period, which is maintained manually in the ward register. That showed something like 96 per cent. We opened the beds. The screen would have told us not to.
Q3_text: I am not a technical person, so I will answer as I see it. There is a time stamp on the report and I assume it is correct. Whether a feed has failed, I honestly do not know how I would come to know from the screen. There is no colour or message of that type that I have noticed. What makes me doubt a report is when it contradicts what the ward sisters are telling me in the morning huddle, and in this hospital I have learnt to believe the sisters first. They have no reason to exaggerate, they are the ones who have to manage with whatever staff is sanctioned.
Q4_text: Yes, more than once, but the one I remember is a pharmacy stock report which showed adequate stock of a particular antibiotic while the ward was telling me they are borrowing from another floor. The report was counting the stock lying in the returns bin which had not been reconciled, so physically the medicine was in the building but it was not usable stock. I asked for a physical count that same evening.
Q5_text: This one I did put on record because in our hospital any medication availability issue goes into the incident reporting system, that is a NABH requirement. So it was logged, the pharmacy in charge had to respond within a defined period, and it came up in the monthly quality committee. The reconciliation process was changed after that. I would say we are better than most organisations on this one point, because the format exists and people use it. But please note it is a clinical safety system. If the same problem had been in a finance report there is no such form and it would have been an email at best.
Q6_text: In a hospital, both carry weight but in different rooms. In the quality and clinical committees, documented evidence is everything, an incident form or an audit finding will move things. In the management review with the finance side, a report is the only currency, and my own reading of the situation is treated as a soft input. And yes, defending a decision with a report is much easier. When we opened those eight beds I was asked to justify it and I had to produce the manual afternoon census in a proper format before it was accepted, even though everybody in the building knew the ward was full.
Q7_text: If I follow the system and something goes wrong clinically, there is still an enquiry, because in healthcare the patient outcome does not care what the roster software said. But the enquiry will be about the system. If I overrule the roster and there is an adverse event, the question becomes why did you deviate, and it is asked in a different tone. I will say the gap is smaller here than in other industries because we have a genuine safety culture, but it is there. Nobody is ever asked why they kept extra staff, though they are asked about the cost later.
Q8_text: Very often. A ward sister told us for weeks that the discharge summaries were being counted as discharges even when the patient physically left the next morning, which was making our turnaround time look better than it was. Q1_text: A sales and margin dashboard in Power BI which refreshes at 6 am, a stock cover report, and a markdown tracker during end of season sale. First thing I look at is the refresh timestamp in the corner, genuinely, because I have been burnt by presenting stale numbers in a morning call. After that it is like for like growth by category and then stock cover for the categories I own.
Q2_text: During the last end of season sale we had to decide the second markdown depth for a set of apparel styles. The dashboard showed sell through at 46 per cent for one style group which put it in the deeper markdown bucket automatically. What I noticed was that about 30 per cent of the stock of those styles was sitting in two warehouses and had never reached the stores, so it could not have sold, and including it in the denominator made the sell through look far worse than the actual store performance. I pulled the store level stock and reran the sell through on stock actually available at store. It came to around 61 per cent. We took a shallower markdown on those styles and saved a reasonable amount of margin. It took me most of a day to establish that, and the automatic recommendation would have taken thirty seconds.
Q3_text: Partly I can tell, because our BI team put a last refreshed stamp on the main dashboards and it turns red if the refresh failed. That covers the daily sales feed. It does not cover the stock feed from the warehouse system, which comes through a different route and has no indicator at all. So my honest answer is that I know the freshness of the number I look at most and I do not know the freshness of half the numbers underneath it. What makes me doubt a number is when the growth figure and the volume figure are moving in directions that cannot both be true.
Q4_text: Yes, the one I described is a version of it, but there was a sharper case. A dashboard showed one store's conversion rate at nearly double the chain average for a month. I did not believe it. The footfall counter at that store's second entrance had failed, so footfall was undercounted, and conversion is sales divided by footfall. Fewer people counted, same sales, wonderful conversion. That store was actually being held up as an example in a regional meeting.
Q5_text: I raised it by email to the retail operations team and to my manager, with the calculation. The counter was fixed within about two weeks. What happened to the report is more interesting, nothing. The store stayed in that month's league table at the inflated figure because the file had already gone out and reissuing an MIS is a bigger deal politically than the error itself. My email exists in an inbox somewhere. There is no place in our systems that records that the conversion metric for that store was invalid for that month. If someone runs a historical analysis next year that store will still look like a star.
Q6_text: A report, without question. And I say that as somebody who produces the reports, which makes me uncomfortable. My own analysis, if it is presented as an analysis with a chart, carries far more weight than the same insight spoken aloud. I have literally taken a point that was rejected in a meeting, put it into a slide with the same numbers, and had it accepted the following week. The content did not change.
Q7_text: Different, clearly. Following the automatic markdown recommendation and losing margin is a system outcome and everybody shrugs. Deviating from it and losing margin is my decision and it will be discussed by name. In the case I described, I deviated, and I made sure the reasoning was in writing before the markdown went live, precisely because I knew that if it went badly the written note was my only protection. That is quite a telling thing to notice about yourself.
Q8_text: Store managers tell us all the time that the stock the system shows is not on the floor, it is in the back room or it is damaged. They log it as a stock query in a portal we have, so it is recorded, which is better than most of the examples I imagine you are collecting. But the queries go to a shared inbox and get resolved individually. Nobody aggregates them, so the pattern that would tell us the process is broken is sitting in three thousand individual tickets and nobody has ever looked at them together. I actually did that once out of curiosity and it was quite alarming.
Q9_text: It narrows it a lot. The markdown tool gives me depth and timing, so we discuss depth and timing. What we never discuss is moving stock between regions, because inter store transfer cost is not in the model, or holding stock for next season, because there is no field for it. Those are sometimes obviously better options and they are not on the table simply because the tool does not have them.
Q10_prompt: In the study you have just completed, in the scenario about a delivery route reporting itself as on target the dashboard indicated that the route was at 96 per cent on time and needed no action, while what you knew locally was that the depot supervisor had reported loads arriving without paperwork. You chose: Ask for a manual reconciliation of inbound arrivals against paperwork at Nashik before deciding.Looking back, what would drive your choice if this were a real decision at your work?
Q10_text: I chose to ask for the manual reconciliation before deciding, and I would do the same at work, mainly because I have been caught by exactly this shape of problem twice. Missing arrival records look like good performance, in the same way that missing footfall looks like good conversion. Any metric where the thing that has gone wrong also removes itself from the denominator is one I do not trust. What would drive the choice in reality is whether I have someone I can ask. Reconciliation means a person at Nashik doing manual work for a day, and asking for that costs me relationship capital, so I would only spend it where the number is load bearing. Here it is, there is a penalty attached to it.
Q11_text: Publish a list of known broken feeds where everybody can see it, updated daily, the way engineering teams have a status page. At present the knowledge of which feed is unreliable lives in the heads of about four analysts. If it were on a page, a category manager could point at it in a meeting and it would not be an accusation, it would just be a fact.
Q12_text: Only that the effort is asymmetric. Accepting the number takes no time. Checking the number took me a full day and I had to justify the day. Until that asymmetry changes, most people will accept, and they are being rational.

First thing I look at is the refresh timestamp in the corner, genuinely, because I have been burnt by presenting stale numbers in a morning call. After that it is like for like growth by category and then stock cover for the categories I own.
Q2_text: During the last end of season sale we had to decide the second markdown depth for a set of apparel styles. The dashboard showed sell through at 46 per cent for one style group which put it in the deeper markdown bucket automatically. What I noticed was that about 30 per cent of the stock of those styles was sitting in two warehouses and had never reached the stores, so it could not have sold, and including it in the denominator made the sell through look far worse than the actual store performance. I pulled the store level stock and reran the sell through on stock actually available at store. It came to around 61 per cent. We took a shallower markdown on those styles and saved a reasonable amount of margin. It took me most of a day to establish that, and the automatic recommendation would have taken thirty seconds.
Q3_text: Partly I can tell, because our BI team put a last refreshed stamp on the main dashboards and it turns red if the refresh failed. That covers the daily sales feed. It does not cover the stock feed from the warehouse system, which comes through a different route and has no indicator at all. So my honest answer is that I know the freshness of the number I look at most and I do not know the freshness of half the numbers underneath it. What makes me doubt a number is when the growth figure and the volume figure are moving in directions that cannot both be true.
Q4_text: Yes, the one I described is a version of it, but there was a sharper case. A dashboard showed one store's conversion rate at nearly double the chain average for a month. I did not believe it. The footfall counter at that store's second entrance had failed, so footfall was undercounted, and conversion is sales divided by footfall. Fewer people counted, same sales, wonderful conversion. That store was actually being held up as an example in a regional meeting.
Q5_text: I raised it by email to the retail operations team and to my manager, with the calculation. The counter was fixed within about two weeks. What happened to the report is more interesting, nothing. The store stayed in that month's league table at the inflated figure because the file had already gone out and reissuing an MIS is a bigger deal politically than the error itself. My email exists in an inbox somewhere. There is no place in our systems that records that the conversion metric for that store was invalid for that month. If someone runs a historical analysis next year that store will still look like a star.
Q6_text: A report, without question. And I say that as somebody who produces the reports, which makes me uncomfortable. My own analysis, if it is presented as an analysis with a chart, carries far more weight than the same insight spoken aloud. I have literally taken a point that was rejected in a meeting, put it into a slide with the same numbers, and had it accepted the following week. The content did not change.
Q7_text: Different, clearly. Following the automatic markdown recommendation and losing margin is a system outcome and everybody shrugs. Deviating from it and losing margin is my decision and it will be discussed by name. In the case I described, I deviated, and I made sure the reasoning was in writing before the markdown went live, precisely because I knew that if it went badly the written note was my only protection. That is quite a telling thing to notice about yourself.
Q8_text: Store managers tell us all the time that the stock the system shows is not on the floor, it is in the back room or it is damaged. They log it as a stock query in a portal we have, so it is recorded, which is better than most of the examples I imagine you are collecting. But the queries go to a shared inbox and get resolved individually. Nobody aggregates them, so the pattern that would tell us the process is broken is sitting in three thousand individual tickets and nobody has ever looked at them together. I actually did that once out of curiosity and it was quite alarming.
Q9_text: It narrows it a lot. The markdown tool gives me depth and timing, so we discuss depth and timing. What we never discuss is moving stock between regions, because inter store transfer cost is not in the model, or holding stock for next season, because there is no field for it. Those are sometimes obviously better options and they are not on the table simply because the tool does not have them.
Q10_prompt: In the study you have just completed, in the scenario about a delivery route reporting itself as on target the dashboard indicated that the route was at 96 per cent on time and needed no action, while what you knew locally was that the depot supervisor had reported loads arriving without paperwork. You chose: Ask for a manual reconciliation of inbound arrivals against paperwork at Nashik before deciding.Looking back, what would drive your choice if this were a real decision at your work?
Q10_text: I chose to ask for the manual reconciliation before deciding, and I would do the same at work, mainly because I have been caught by exactly this shape of problem twice. Missing arrival records look like good performance, in the same way that missing footfall looks like good conversion. Any metric where the thing that has gone wrong also removes itself from the denominator is one I do not trust. What would drive the choice in reality is whether I have someone I can ask. Reconciliation means a person at Nashik doing manual work for a day, and asking for that costs me relationship capital, so I would only spend it where the number is load bearing. Here it is, there is a penalty attached to it.
Q11_text: Publish a list of known broken feeds where everybody can see it, updated daily, the way engineering teams have a status page. At present the knowledge of which feed is unreliable lives in the heads of about four analysts. If it were on a page, a category manager could point at it in a meeting and it would not be an accusation, it would just be a fact.
Q12_text: Only that the effort is asymmetric. Accepting the number takes no time. Checking the number took me a full day and I had to justify the day. Until that asymmetry changes, most people will accept, and they are being rational.

Decision making with business intelligence tools and how much we trust them.
Q1_text: I open the model monitoring dashboard first thing, that is a Tableau workbook, and then a portfolio delinquency view in Power BI. Also I keep a Databricks notebook running for ad hoc checks. On the monitoring one, the first thing I look at is the population stability index panel and the record counts by month, because if the counts look off then nothing below it is worth reading. Most of my colleagues look at the AUC first. I have learnt to look at the denominator first.
Q2_text: Two months back there was a decision on whether to keep a scorecard live or fall back to the previous version. The dashboard showed a sharp drop in approval rate for one segment and the automatic flag said model drift. What I noticed first was that the drop was completely concentrated in one sourcing channel and it started on a Monday, exactly. Drift does not start on a Monday, a release does. I checked the raw feed and the bureau attributes for that channel were coming as null after a vendor API change. So the model was fine, the input was broken. We fixed the feed and kept the model live. Had we gone by the dashboard we would have rolled back a perfectly good scorecard and spent two months rebuilding it.
Q3_text: For my own dashboards I know, because I built the checks myself. There is a small panel showing last load time and row counts by day, and it goes amber if the load is more than 26 hours old. That is not standard in our bank, it is something our team added after the incident I described. The business dashboards that go to the sales side have nothing of this sort, they just show the number. So the answer is yes sometimes, and only where somebody took the trouble. What makes me doubt a number is a perfectly flat line, or a distribution that has not moved at all when I know the underlying population has changed.
Q4_text: Yes. A recovery dashboard was showing collection efficiency improving for four straight weeks in one bucket. I did not believe it because the field teams were on strike in one region for part of that period, so the improvement was arithmetically impossible. It turned out that the accounts from that region were dropping out of the denominator because of a status code that was not being mapped. So efficiency looked better simply because the difficult accounts had disappeared from the report.
Q5_text: I raised it with my reporting manager and then in the data quality forum which meets fortnightly. It was taken well, to be fair, and a ticket was raised. The ticket is the only record. There is a JIRA number and a resolution comment, but nobody outside the data team will ever see it, and the business MIS that went out for those four weeks was never corrected or recalled. So partly recorded, and partly not. As such the outcome was good, the mapping was fixed. Having said that, if I had not noticed, nothing would have happened, and that is the uncomfortable part.
Q6_text: Evidence means a number with a source. If you can say this came from the warehouse table and here is the query, the discussion closes. Personal judgement carries weight only if you are senior, and even then people will politely ask for the supporting data. For someone at my level judgement alone carries almost nothing. Q1_text: An engagement portfolio dashboard covering margin, utilisation and delivery status across the accounts I am responsible for, plus a client facing programme dashboard on the largest of them. The first thing I look at on my own portfolio is the status colour that has not changed for several weeks. A project that has been amber for two months is telling you something quite different from one that went amber last Friday, and the dashboard treats them identically.
Q2_text: We had to decide whether to reset the plan on a programme that was reporting green on delivery but where I had a feeling from the last steering committee that the client was uneasy. The dashboard showed milestones being met. What I checked was the composition of the milestones, and it turned out that the ones being met were internal deliverables while the two that involved client sign off had been rescheduled twice, and rescheduling resets the due date so it never shows as late. I asked for a list of every milestone that had ever been moved. That list looked nothing like the dashboard. We reset the plan and had a difficult conversation early, which was much better than having it late.
Q3_text: Only partially. Our internal financial dashboards carry a data as at date and they are reliable because finance owns them. The delivery status dashboards are self reported by project managers, and there is no indicator distinguishing a status that was reviewed this week from one that has simply been carried forward. That is the gap. The status field is never empty, so it always looks current. I would rather have a screen that admits it does not know than one that quietly repeats itself.
Q4_text: Yes, the milestone case above is one. An earlier one that stays with me was a client's own operations dashboard which showed a call centre meeting its service level comfortably, while every conversation I had in the building suggested it was in real difficulty. Abandoned calls before a threshold were excluded from the calculation, and the abandonment rate had risen sharply. The service level was true and irrelevant.
Q5_text: On the client's dashboard, I raised it with the programme sponsor and put it in a formal note in the risk section of our report, which is minuted at the steering committee, so it was recorded. The sponsor's response was to ask the operations director to comment, which he did, defensively, and the definition was eventually changed about four months later after a customer complaint reached the board. So it was recorded and it was answered, but the answer was a defence rather than a change, and the change came from outside. That sequence is very common in my experience. The objection is recorded, the answer is a rebuttal, and the actual change is triggered by an external event some months later.
Q6_text: In consulting, a documented analysis carries enormous weight, partly because it is also a commercial artefact. And I would say the effect is stronger with clients than internally. Internally, a partner's judgement is still currency. With a client, judgement without evidence is what they are paying us not to give them. So yes, a decision backed by a report is easier to defend, and there is a slightly cynical corollary, which is that the report also transfers the risk. Both parties know that the existence of the analysis protects everyone in the room if it goes wrong.
Q7_text: For me they are closer than they would have been fifteen years ago, largely because at director level you are expected to have a view. But the asymmetry has not disappeared, it has moved. If I follow the reported status and a programme fails, the question is about governance. If I overrule the reported status, intervene, and it turns out the programme was fine, that is expensive and visible and I will have burnt goodwill with a client team. So the risk of intervening is real, it is just commercial rather than disciplinary. I suspect that is why intervention happens late almost everywhere.
Q8_text: A test lead on one programme told us for weeks that the defect numbers were understated because failures were being logged as queries and queries were not counted. She raised it with the programme manager. It was noted in a weekly report as an observation. Nothing was answered. She then raised it with me directly, somewhat reluctantly, and I put it into the steering pack, at which point it became a formal issue and was resolved in a fortnight. What troubles me is that it needed her to go around her own manager to a client director. The formal route existed and it did not work at her level. It worked at mine.
Q9_text: Very much so. The portfolio dashboard shows margin, utilisation and status, so my management conversations are about staffing and scope. What does not appear anywhere is whether the engagement is doing the client any good, which is the thing that actually determines whether they call us again. There is no tile for that, and so the discussion happens only when someone raises it deliberately, usually me, usually last on the agenda.
Q10_prompt: In the study you have just completed, in the scenario about a delivery route reporting itself as on target the dashboard indicated that the route was at 96 per cent on time and needed no action, while what you knew locally was that the depot supervisor had reported loads arriving without paperwork. You chose: Take no action. The route is green and within service level.Looking back, what would drive your choice if this were a real decision at your work?
Q10_text: I chose to take no action on the freight route, and having spent the last twenty minutes writing about milestone dates that never show as late, I find that quite instructive. The pattern was identical, a measure that looks healthy because the failing cases have been removed from it, and I did not see it. I think the reason is that it was presented as a logistics operations problem and I read it as somebody else's specialism, so I accepted the frame the screen offered. What would drive the choice in a real situation is whether I have any reason to distrust the measure. Twelve per cent of arrival records missing is a reason and it was in front of me. Being outside your own domain does not make you cautious. It appears to make you compliant, which is the opposite of what one would hope.
Q11_text: One change, and it is a governance change rather than a technical one. Require every reported status to carry the date it was last independently checked, not the date it was last edited. That single field would expose most of what I have described, because a status that has never been checked would be visible as such, and nobody would have to accuse anybody of anything to raise it.
Q12_text: One reflection. You have asked, quite rightly, about what happens when someone disagrees with a dashboard. In my experience the more common and more damaging case is that nobody disagrees, because the dashboard has quietly redefined what the question is. By the time a number is on a screen in a steering committee, the argument about what should be measured is already over, and it was usually settled by whoever built the report. That is where the power sits and it is almost never examined.

Q1_text: Production dashboard on the shop floor display and one shift report which I have to fill and send. Also OEE screen. First thing I see is the production count against the shift target because that is the first question my HOD asks in the morning meeting.
Q2_text: Last month there was a decision on whether to run the third shift on Saturday. The dashboard was showing pending order quantity and as per that we needed the extra shift. I checked the pending order figure and the manpower availability. Then I put up the requirement to my HOD and he approved. Actually the decision was his, I only put up the numbers as the system showed.
Q3_text: I cannot say. The system data comes automatically from the machines so we assume it is correct. Sometimes the count is showing less because one machine counter is not working, then the operator tells us and we correct manually in the shift report. But on the dashboard it stays wrong. There is no warning coming. Only the operator knows.
Q4_text: Yes one time the OEE was showing 82 per cent for our line which was very high. Everyone was saying good. But actually one machine was not running that day so it was not counted at all, so the average of the remaining machines went up. I told my senior about it.
Q5_text: I told him verbally. He said okay and that was all. Nothing was written. Next month the same thing happened again. In our plant there is no system for writing such things, we only have the shift report format and there is no column for this.
Q6_text: Report is easier for sure. If the system shows something then nobody questions. If I say something from my side then they will ask what is your basis. So better to show the report only.
Q7_text: Very different sir. If I follow the system nobody will say anything to me. If I do something on my own and it goes wrong then it will come in my confirmation review and my HOD will say why did you not ask. I am only two years in this company so I cannot take that chance. Even if I feel the number is wrong I will put it up as it is and mention verbally that there may be an issue.
Q8_text: Operators say many times that the count is not matching. They tell the supervisor. Supervisor tells us if he remembers. Nothing is written anywhere.
Q9_text: Yes because we only look at what is on the screen. Manpower, overtime, machine availability. We never discuss changing the product sequence because that is planning department's work and we do not have that screen.
Q10_prompt: In the study you have just completed, in the scenario about deferring a plant shutdown the dashboard indicated that the line was healthy and the shutdown could be deferred to December, while what you knew locally was that the shift engineer had reported knocking from a mill whose sensor was never calibrated. You chose: Defer the shutdown to December, as the health index supports.Looking back, what would drive your choice if this were a real decision at your work?
Q10_text: I chose to defer the shutdown as the health index was showing good. Honestly if my HOD asks me to put up a note I will put up what the system is showing, because that is what is expected. The shift engineer's complaint about knocking sound is a verbal thing, I cannot write in a note that somebody heard a sound. If I write that and the shutdown is postponed anyway then I have wasted everyone's time. And if I recommend spending three crore because of a sound and nothing is found, then it will be remembered. So mainly it is about what I can defend if somebody asks me later.
Q11_text: If the system itself shows the sensor is not calibrated then it is easy for us. Otherwise it is difficult for a junior person to say anything.
