suspicion_text: Whether accountability pressure makes people hide behind the report.
level: Senior manager or head of function
Q1_text: We are not a very dashboard heavy place. There is an ERP module with admission and attendance data, and I look at a student enrolment summary and a fee collection status report. During accreditation season there is a separate data sheet for NIRF and NAAC which is compiled by hand from several sources. When the enrolment report opens I look at programme wise vacancy against sanctioned intake, because everything else in my work follows from that number.
Q2_text: We had to decide whether to run an elective in the odd semester with a small cohort. The system showed 14 registrations against a minimum of 20, and the automatic recommendation in the ERP was to withdraw the course. What I noticed is that our registration window closes before the supplementary results are declared, so students who are yet to clear a prerequisite cannot register even though many of them will clear it. I asked the examination section for the pending list and roughly 11 more students were eligible once the results came. We ran the course and it had 23 students. The system was working correctly and the calendar was the problem, but the effect on the decision was the same.
Q3_text: Frankly I do not know how to tell, and I am not sure anyone here does. The ERP was implemented by a vendor and we were trained on data entry, not on how the reports are built. There is no message about stale data that I have seen. My way of checking is to ask the section that owns the data, so for enrolment I ask the admission cell and for attendance I ask the department. If the two do not agree then I know one of them is wrong, and usually the ERP figure is the older one because entries are made in batches at the end of the month.
Q4_text: Yes. The attendance dashboard showed one department with 94 per cent average attendance which was simply not credible, we all walk past those classrooms. What had happened is that faculty were marking attendance at the end of the month from memory rather than daily in the app, and when you fill it from memory you fill it generously. So the data was entered, it was complete, and it was fiction.
Q5_text: I raised it verbally with the head of that department and then in the academic monitoring committee. Nothing was written specifically. The head was defensive, which I expected, because attendance is tied to eligibility for the examination and there are consequences for students. What happened in the end is that we made the app mark entries with a timestamp so that late entry becomes visible. That took about a year and it happened because of an audit query, not because of my point. My objection was not recorded anywhere. If you asked the committee today, nobody would remember I raised it.
Q6_text: In a university, a document carries weight, but the document that carries weight is the one required by a statute or by the accreditation body. A report generated internally has much less standing than a minute of a statutory body. So a decision backed by a report is somewhat easier to defend, but a decision backed by a resolution is very much easier. My own judgement, after twenty two years, carries some weight in the corridor and almost none in the file. That is the honest position and it is a little disappointing to write it down.
Q7_text: If I follow the system and the outcome is poor, it is treated as a procedural matter. If I withdraw or run a course against what the system recommends and it goes badly, then it is my decision and it will be raised in the next review, sometimes years later when the cohort's results come out. The asymmetry is large. I would add that in academia the timescales are so long that the person who took the decision is often no longer in that seat, which paradoxically makes people more cautious, not less, because they know the record will outlive them.
Q8_text: Our clerks in the examination section know the data better than anyone. One of them told us repeatedly that the mapping of elective courses to credits was wrong for one programme, which would affect the transcripts. He told his section officer. It went nowhere for two semesters. It surfaced when a student going abroad had a transcript query and then it was fixed in a week. Nobody recorded that he had raised it. When it was fixed the credit was taken by the committee that fixed it. I remember thinking that if we had a place to write these things, that clerk would have three years of correct predictions to his name.
Q9_text: Yes it does. The ERP gives me registrations, vacancy and fee status, so my options are run the course, withdraw it, or merge sections. What is never on the table is changing when the registration window opens, which as I explained is the actual cause of the problem. The system cannot show me a decision that is about the system's own timing, so that option has to be raised by a human being who has noticed, and most people are too busy to notice.
Q10_prompt: In the study you have just completed, in the scenario about renewing a supplier at increased volume the dashboard indicated that the supplier scored 98.6 per cent and should be renewed at higher volume, while what you knew locally was that the inspector had been passing batches by eye because the test rig was out of calibration. You chose: Move volume to the second-ranked supplier instead.Looking back, what would drive your choice if this were a real decision at your work?
Q10_text: I chose to move the volume to the second ranked supplier, which I notice is neither accepting nor checking. Looking back that was a way of avoiding the argument. It removes the immediate risk and it does not require me to challenge anybody's scorecard, and I think that is a very administrative instinct, to route around a problem rather than to name it. In my own work the equivalent would be quietly not running a course rather than saying the eligibility data is wrong. What would drive the real decision is whether naming the problem creates a conflict with a colleague I have to work with for the next ten years. In a small institution that consideration is much heavier than people outside understand.
Q11_text: A place to record a doubt that does not require an accusation. In our culture, questioning a number is heard as questioning a colleague's integrity, because the number was entered by a person sitting two rooms away. Until it is possible to say this figure looks doubtful without it becoming personal, people will simply stay quiet, and no amount of software will change that.
Q12_text: Perhaps that you should consider institutions where the data is entered by the same people who are judged by it. That is our situation and I suspect it is common in the public sector generally. The problem is not that people do not trust the dashboard. It is that everybody knows exactly how the dashboard is made.

role: Manager with budget or people responsibility
seniority: Senior manager or head of function
suspicion_text: Whether senior people and junior people read the same dashboard differently.
job_title: Head of Category - Home and Personal Care
level: Senior manager or head of function
Q1_text: Every morning it is the category performance dashboard, sales value, volume, and rate of sale by store cluster. Then twice a week the inventory and ageing report, and once a week the competition price tracker which a third party agency provides. On the main dashboard my eye goes straight to rate of sale for my top twenty SKUs, not to the total. Total sales can look fine while three SKUs are carrying everything, and that is the situation that hurts you two months later.
Q2_text: Last quarter we were deciding whether to expand a shampoo sachet range into 400 more stores. The dashboard showed strong sell through, something like 78 per cent, in the pilot cluster, and the recommendation engine had already ranked those stores for expansion. What I noticed first was that the pilot period overlapped with a large consumer promotion, so the sell through was bought, not earned. I asked the team for the non promo weeks separately, and I asked two of our territory managers to tell me what the shelf looked like. On non promo weeks sell through was around 41 per cent. We did a smaller expansion of 120 stores instead and it has done reasonably. If I had gone with the screen we would have had dead stock across 400 stores by Diwali.
Q3_text: I cannot tell from the screen at all, and I have stopped assuming. Our dashboards do not show any warning about the feed. The one clue we have is that certain stores go missing from the store list, and you only notice that if you know the count of stores you should be seeing, which most people do not. Secondary sales data comes from distributors and it is late almost every month during closing, but the dashboard does not say late, it simply shows a lower number, and then everybody panics for two days until the data lands. That happens every single month and we have still not put a message on the screen.
Q4_text: Yes, and it is the same theme. The dashboard showed one region's offtake dropping by nearly 30 per cent in a month. I did not believe it because I had been in that market ten days before and the shelves were moving. What had happened was that a large distributor in that region had changed to a new billing system and their data was not flowing. So the market was fine, the pipe was broken. But for those ten days our sales team was being questioned in the review for a collapse that had not happened.
Q5_text: I raised it on the review call itself, in front of everybody, which was probably not the polite way but it stopped people being pulled up unfairly. The IT and commercial teams took it up and the feed was fixed in about a week. Written down, no. There was no correction note, no revised MIS. The regional manager who had already been marked down in that month's review was never formally un-marked. The numbers were restated quietly in the next month's file and that was the end of it. Nobody said sorry and nobody recorded that the report had been wrong.
Q6_text: A report wins, easily. In our organisation the review culture is built entirely on the MIS pack. If your point is not in the pack, it is an opinion, and opinions are heard last if the meeting is running late, which it always is. I will give you a concrete example. My argument for the smaller expansion was accepted only after I put the promo adjusted sell through into a slide. The same argument made verbally two weeks earlier had gone nowhere. Same content, same person, different container.
Q7_text: They are absolutely not the same, and I would say the gap is the single biggest thing shaping behaviour in my function. If I follow the recommendation and the range fails, it is a market issue, the model gets tuned, we all move on. If I overrule the recommendation and it fails, it becomes a story about my judgement and it will be brought up in the next planning cycle. So people learn to follow, and if they disagree they follow anyway and mention their concern verbally so that they can say later that they had said so. That verbal caveat is very common and it is useless because it is not recorded.
Q8_text: Our territory managers are the ones closest to the ground and they are the least likely to be believed. One of them told us that a competitor was doing a heavy consumer offer in his towns, three months before it showed in our price tracker, because the tracker only covers modern trade and this was a general trade offer. He said it on calls, he even sent photographs. Nothing was recorded. The photographs went into a WhatsApp group. The tracker eventually picked it up and by then we had lost about two months of share. If somebody had written down what he said on the day he said it, we would at least be able to show that the intelligence existed.
Q9_text: It narrows it very sharply and I have become quite conscious of this. The dashboard gives me price, promotion, distribution and assortment, so those four become the entire discussion. What almost never comes up is anything about pack architecture or reformulation, because there is no tile for it and no forecast attached to it, so proposing it feels like speculation. Also anything involving a specific retailer relationship never appears, because it is qualitative. The screen has made us very good at tactical moves and quite poor at structural ones.
Q10_prompt: In the study you have just completed, in the scenario about cutting a hospital night shift the dashboard indicated that admissions would fall 22 per cent and the shift could drop from six nurses to four, while what you knew locally was that the ward sister said the feeder clinics were sending patients as usual. You chose: Cut the night shift to four nurses for the coming week, as the rota system recommends.Looking back, what would drive your choice if this were a real decision at your work?
Q10_text: I chose to cut the night shift as the system recommended, and I noticed while doing the later situations that I had answered that first one much too fast. Once I realised the briefs contained something the screen did not know, I started reading them properly, and my answers changed completely after that. That is quite revealing about how I actually work. First screen of the day, I trust it. By the third one I am checking. In a real situation what would drive it is the cost of being wrong in each direction, and for a nursing rota that is completely asymmetric, four nurses on a post operative ward is not something you experiment with to save agency cost. I would not make that decision again the same way.
Q11_text: Change what gets asked in the review, not the tool. If the first question from the leadership in every monthly review was which numbers in this pack are you least confident about, the entire behaviour would change in one quarter. At present the first question is always why is this red, so everybody arrives ready to defend the number rather than to interrogate it. The tool follows the meeting, not the other way round.
Q12_text: One thing. Please do look at how quickly people answer. I answered your first situation in what felt like twenty seconds and I would have defended that answer if you had asked me. Speed is a big part of this and I am not sure surveys usually capture it.

level: Senior manager or head of function
Q1_text: Every morning it is the category performance dashboard, sales value, volume, and rate of sale by store cluster. Then twice a week the inventory and ageing report, and once a week the competition price tracker which a third party agency provides. On the main dashboard my eye goes straight to rate of sale for my top twenty SKUs, not to the total. Total sales can look fine while three SKUs are carrying everything, and that is the situation that hurts you two months later.
Q2_text: Last quarter we were deciding whether to expand a shampoo sachet range into 400 more stores. The dashboard showed strong sell through, something like 78 per cent, in the pilot cluster, and the recommendation engine had already ranked those stores for expansion. What I noticed first was that the pilot period overlapped with a large consumer promotion, so the sell through was bought, not earned. I asked the team for the non promo weeks separately, and I asked two of our territory managers to tell me what the shelf looked like. On non promo weeks sell through was around 41 per cent. We did a smaller expansion of 120 stores instead and it has done reasonably. If I had gone with the screen we would have had dead stock across 400 stores by Diwali.
Q3_text: I cannot tell from the screen at all, and I have stopped assuming. Our dashboards do not show any warning about the feed. The one clue we have is that certain stores go missing from the store list, and you only notice that if you know the count of stores you should be seeing, which most people do not. Secondary sales data comes from distributors and it is late almost every month during closing, but the dashboard does not say late, it simply shows a lower number, and then everybody panics for two days until the data lands. That happens every single month and we have still not put a message on the screen.
Q4_text: Yes, and it is the same theme. The dashboard showed one region's offtake dropping by nearly 30 per cent in a month. I did not believe it because I had been in that market ten days before and the shelves were moving. What had happened was that a large distributor in that region had changed to a new billing system and their data was not flowing. So the market was fine, the pipe was broken. But for those ten days our sales team was being questioned in the review for a collapse that had not happened.
Q5_text: I raised it on the review call itself, in front of everybody, which was probably not the polite way but it stopped people being pulled up unfairly. The IT and commercial teams took it up and the feed was fixed in about a week. Written down, no. There was no correction note, no revised MIS. The regional manager who had already been marked down in that month's review was never formally un-marked. The numbers were restated quietly in the next month's file and that was the end of it. Nobody said sorry and nobody recorded that the report had been wrong.
Q6_text: A report wins, easily. In our organisation the review culture is built entirely on the MIS pack. If your point is not in the pack, it is an opinion, and opinions are heard last if the meeting is running late, which it always is. I will give you a concrete example. My argument for the smaller expansion was accepted only after I put the promo adjusted sell through into a slide. The same argument made verbally two weeks earlier had gone nowhere. Same content, same person, different container.
Q7_text: They are absolutely not the same, and I would say the gap is the single biggest thing shaping behaviour in my function. If I follow the recommendation and the range fails, it is a market issue, the model gets tuned, we all move on. If I overrule the recommendation and it fails, it becomes a story about my judgement and it will be brought up in the next planning cycle. So people learn to follow, and if they disagree they follow anyway and mention their concern verbally so that they can say later that they had said so. That verbal caveat is very common and it is useless because it is not recorded.
Q8_text: Our territory managers are the ones closest to the ground and they are the least likely to be believed. One of them told us that a competitor was doing a heavy consumer offer in his towns, three months before it showed in our price tracker, because the tracker only covers modern trade and this was a general trade offer. He said it on calls, he even sent photographs. Nothing was recorded. The photographs went into a WhatsApp group. The tracker eventually picked it up and by then we had lost about two months of share. If somebody had written down what he said on the day he said it, we would at least be able to show that the intelligence existed.
Q9_text: It narrows it very sharply and I have become quite conscious of this. The dashboard gives me price, promotion, distribution and assortment, so those four become the entire discussion. What almost never comes up is anything about pack architecture or reformulation, because there is no tile for it and no forecast attached to it, so proposing it feels like speculation. Also anything involving a specific retailer relationship never appears, because it is qualitative. The screen has made us very good at tactical moves and quite poor at structural ones.
Q10_prompt: In the study you have just completed, in the scenario about cutting a hospital night shift the dashboard indicated that admissions would fall 22 per cent and the shift could drop from six nurses to four, while what you knew locally was that the ward sister said the feeder clinics were sending patients as usual. You chose: Cut the night shift to four nurses for the coming week, as the rota system recommends.Looking back, what would drive your choice if this were a real decision at your work?
Q10_text: I chose to cut the night shift as the system recommended, and I noticed while doing the later situations that I had answered that first one much too fast. Once I realised the briefs contained something the screen did not know, I started reading them properly, and my answers changed completely after that. That is quite revealing about how I actually work. First screen of the day, I trust it. By the third one I am checking. In a real situation what would drive it is the cost of being wrong in each direction, and for a nursing rota that is completely asymmetric, four nurses on a post operative ward is not something you experiment with to save agency cost. I would not make that decision again the same way.
Q11_text: Change what gets asked in the review, not the tool. If the first question from the leadership in every monthly review was which numbers in this pack are you least confident about, the entire behaviour would change in one quarter. At present the first question is always why is this red, so everybody arrives ready to defend the number rather than to interrogate it. The tool follows the meeting, not the other way round.
Q12_text: One thing. Please do look at how quickly people answer. I answered your first situation in what felt like twenty seconds and I would have defended that answer if you had asked me. Speed is a big part of this and I am not sure surveys usually capture it.

level: Senior manager or head of function
Q1_text: SCADA screens in the control room and one daily generation and outage report which comes on mail. Also the maintenance module in SAP for pending work orders. First look is at the availability figure and the list of forced outages for the previous day. Nothing else matters if there is an outage.
Q2_text: We had to decide whether to take a transformer out for maintenance before the monsoon or after. The report showed oil test parameters within limits and the health index was good. But the site engineer had noted higher temperature on two occasions in the log book, which is not in any system, it is a physical register. I asked for the thermography report which is done quarterly and it showed a hot spot on one bushing. We took it out in May itself and found the connection was loose. Had we waited we would have had a failure in the rains.
Q3_text: No system tells you this. The data comes from the RTU and if the RTU is not communicating, the last value simply remains on the screen. It does not go blank. This is a known thing in our field, an old value looks exactly like a live value. Only the control room operator knows because he is watching continuously. Our reports have no warning of any kind. What makes me doubt is when a value is exactly constant. In a running plant nothing is ever exactly constant.
Q4_text: Yes many times. Most recent one, the auxiliary consumption figure was showing a nice reduction for one month. Not believable, because nothing had changed in the operation. One meter was under repair and its consumption was simply not getting added. So the saving was actually a missing meter.
Q5_text: I informed the MIS section and the figure was revised in the next month's report. Written down, no. It was a phone call and then a corrected file. Nobody records that the earlier report was wrong. The wrong figure had already gone to the head office monthly review by then and it was appreciated as an improvement. Nobody went back and told them. This happens more than people think.
Q6_text: Report is stronger, definitely. In our review meetings if it is not in the MIS then it is not discussed. My own assessment is asked for only when something has already gone wrong. Then everybody wants the field view.
Q7_text: Not the same. Follow the report and there is a problem, it is a system issue and there is a committee. Go against the report and there is a problem, you will have to explain in writing why you deviated. So people follow. Simple. Though I will say in maintenance we have some freedom because safety is accepted as a reason. If I say it is unsafe, nobody argues with me. That word protects us.
Q8_text: The shift engineers and the technicians know first, always. They tell in the shift handover. It goes in the log book which is a physical register kept in the control room. That is a record technically but nobody above the shift level reads it. If it is serious the shift engineer will call me directly. If it is a small thing it stays in the book and the book goes to the store room after a year.
Q9_text: Yes. The screen shows me availability, outage hours and cost. So we discuss shifting the outage, extending the outage, or doing partial work. What is never discussed is running at reduced load for some period, because the generation loss is somebody else's number and it does not come on my screen. Commercially it may be the best option in some cases but it never comes up in our meeting.
Q10_prompt: In the study you have just completed, in the scenario about a delivery route reporting itself as on target the dashboard indicated that the route was at 96 per cent on time and needed no action, while what you knew locally was that the depot supervisor had reported loads arriving without paperwork. You chose: Take no action. The route is green and within service level.Looking back, what would drive your choice if this were a real decision at your work?
Q10_text: I selected no action for the delivery route. In an office situation I might do the same because the number was well within the limit and there is a cost to raising an alarm every time. But in my actual work I would not, because the supervisor calling twice is exactly the pattern we see before a failure. The man on the ground calls, the system says normal, and two weeks later there is an event. I have seen it many times. What drives it for me is whether the person reporting has anything to gain by reporting it. The depot man has nothing to gain by making trouble for himself, so I would believe him.
Q11_text: Show the communication status of the source on the report itself. If the report says this meter last communicated three days back, the whole conversation changes. Right now to prove a number is wrong I have to do a physical check first and only then anybody listens.
Q12_text: Nothing further.

Q1_text: Mainly Amplitude and one Metabase dashboard our team built for daily active users and funnel drop offs. I open Metabase first because it loads faster. First thing I see is DAU and then the signup funnel, mainly to check if yesterday's number is normal or not.
Q2_text: We had to decide whether to keep a new onboarding screen or remove it. The dashboard showed completion rate dropped from 62 to 54 after we launched it. I checked the numbers by device and by day. Actually I mostly just confirmed the drop was real and not a one day thing. Then I put it in the sprint review and the PM decided to roll it back. I did not check anything about the tracking itself, which I now realise I probably should have.
Q3_text: Honestly I have not thought about this much. I assume the data is fine because the dashboard is built by our data team. If something is broken usually someone posts in the slack channel. There is no warning on the dashboard as such, at least I have not seen one. What would make me doubt is if the number is zero, then obviously something is broken. If it is just lower I would assume it is real.
Q4_text: One time the retention chart showed week 4 retention going up a lot which everyone was happy about. It turned out some internal test accounts were included after a change in the filter. I did not catch it, a senior person on the data team caught it.
Q5_text: They fixed the filter and reposted the chart in the channel. Nothing was written down anywhere formally. It was just a slack message saying ignore the earlier chart. To be fair it got fixed fast. But if you search for it now you will not find it, the messages are gone after 90 days on our plan.
Q6_text: Data. Fully data. If you say something in a meeting without a number people will just say can you pull the numbers. Which is fair I guess. But it also means whoever can pull numbers fastest wins the argument, and that is usually not the person who knows the customer best.
Q7_text: I am pretty junior so nobody is really holding me responsible for decisions. But from what I see, if you follow the data and it does not work out then it is fine, we say we learned something. If someone goes against the data and it does not work out then people remember it for a long time. Our PM did that once and it still gets brought up as a joke.
Q8_text: Our support team keeps saying users are confused by a particular flow. They say it in every monthly call. It is not recorded anywhere except their own notion page which our team does not read. Nothing has happened about it for like 8 months. Then last month we ran a usability test and found exactly the same thing and now it is a priority. So basically it needed to come from a study and not from support.
Q9_text: Yes definitely. We only look at what is instrumented. If an event is not tracked then that behaviour basically does not exist for us. There was a whole thing users do with a workaround in the app and we had zero visibility on it because we never added the event. Options that dont show up on the dashboard never get discussed in planning.

If I said hold on there might be a data issue, someone would ask me to prove it and I would not be able to. So mostly what would drive it is that I dont have the standing to say the data is wrong. Maybe in 3 years I will answer differently.

Q12_text: Not really. It was interesting, made me think a bit about how much I just take the chart at face value.

First thing my eye goes to is the plan versus actual column for the previous day, and after that the red cells in the line-wise output. I am honest, I look for red only. If everything is green I close it in half a minute and go for the shop floor round.
Q2_text: Last month we had to decide whether to shift one component line to the second shift or not. The screen was showing capacity utilisation at 78 per cent for that line, so on paper there was room. What I noticed first was that the 78 was an average of four weeks and two of those weeks the line was down for a mould change, so the recent weeks were much tighter. I pulled the daily numbers into Excel and checked week by week. Then I also called the line supervisor and asked how many hours they are actually getting after changeovers. Based on that I did not shift the line, I released overtime instead for two weeks. If I had gone only by the 78 I would have taken a wrong call.
Q3_text: Frankly speaking there is no way to know from the screen. The refresh timestamp is there in one corner but it shows when the report ran, not whether the data came. Twice we have seen the report run happily with half the machines not reporting, because the OPC tags were down, and the dashboard just showed lower production which everyone read as a bad day. Our tools do not display any warning of that kind. Nothing. I come to know only when a supervisor tells me the number is wrong. What makes me doubt is when a number is too round or does not move at all for two or three days, that is usually a dead tag.
Q4_text: Yes, in April. The scrap dashboard showed scrap on one machining line at 0.4 per cent which would be the best we have ever done. I did not believe it because I had personally seen two bins of rejected housings that same week near the CNC section. I asked the quality engineer and it turned out the rejections were being booked under a different cost centre after a small SAP change, so they were simply not landing in that report at all. The number was not wrong, it was just incomplete, which is worse in a way because it looked believable.
Q5_text: I raised it in the daily review call and also on WhatsApp to the quality head. The quality engineer accepted it and the mapping was corrected in about ten days. But your question is whether it was written anywhere, and no, it was not. There is no place in our system where I can say that this report was wrong for three weeks. The corrected number simply appeared and the old numbers stayed as they were in the archive. Nobody went back and told the management that the April figure they had appreciated in the review was not real. That part still bothers me a little.
Q6_text: A report carries much more weight, no doubt. If I say in a review that the line is struggling because I have seen it, the next question will be show me the data. If I put the same thing in a slide with a trend line, it is accepted. Both parts of your question are the same answer here. Example is the overtime approval I mentioned, my verbal request was pending for a week, the moment I attached the week-wise utilisation chart it was approved in one day. Same information only, only the format changed.
Q7_text: They are not the same at all. If I follow the system and it goes wrong, the discussion is about fixing the system, and my name comes up only as who ran it. If I overrule the system and it goes wrong, then it is a personal thing, why did you take that decision on your own, who authorised. I have seen it happen to a colleague in maintenance. So the safe route is always to do what the report says and keep the mail trail. That is the honest reality, whatever the policy may say.
Q8_text: Our line supervisors do it all the time. One of them kept saying the cycle time in the standard is not achievable on that machine after the spindle was changed. He said it in every shift handover for two months. Nobody wrote it down anywhere. It was only when the OEE dropped enough for the plant head to ask questions that an industrial engineering study was done, and the study said exactly what the supervisor had been saying. So it was heard eventually but through the numbers, not through him. Written down, no. Handover registers are there but nobody reads them upward.
Q9_text: It does narrow it, yes. The screen gives me capacity, manpower and overtime, so my discussion becomes about those three. What never comes on the table is changing the sequence of the schedule or talking to the customer for a two-day extension, because that is not costed anywhere in the system. Rescheduling with the customer is often the cheapest option and it is the one we discuss last, if at all, because there is no number for it on any screen.
Q10_prompt: In the study you have just completed, in the scenario about a fraud review queue that had gone quiet the dashboard indicated that the queue was clear and the ageing indicator was green, while what you knew locally was that two analysts had had almost nothing to review since a weekend release. You chose: Report the improvement. The queue is clear and the indicator is green.Looking back, what would drive your choice if this were a real decision at your work?
Q10_text: Looking back I think I answered that one too quickly, and I was also in the mood that the queue being clear is somebody else's good news to report. In my own work I would not do it that way. Two analysts saying they have nothing to review is exactly the kind of thing I take seriously, because operators knowing something is wrong before the system shows it is the normal case in a plant, not the exception. What would actually drive it at my work is whether I have to sign the report. If my name goes on a weekly number and it is later found to be an intake failure, I am the one explaining it. So I would hold it one day and ask the IT team to confirm, and I would put that in writing so the delay is on record.
Q11_text: One thing only, and it is not a tool thing. The report should show me when a source last sent data, plainly, at the top, not buried. Half our problems are that we cannot tell a genuine zero from a missing zero. If the screen said clearly that three of twenty two machines have not reported today, the argument in the review would change completely, because then I am not arguing against the report, I am pointing at what the report itself is admitting.
Q12_text: One thing maybe. In our set up the person who knows the data is wrong is usually two or three levels below the person who is reading the dashboard, and there is nothing connecting the two except somebody's willingness to speak in a call. Whatever solution comes out of your study, it has to work for that supervisor, not only for managers like me.

First thing I check is pending picklist count and the dock utilisation, because that decides whether I have to call for extra manpower or not. Also there is one SLA screen showing on time dispatch percentage which my reporting manager sees, so I check that before he checks it.
Q2_text: Two weeks back the manpower planning sheet showed that the evening shift was overstaffed by six people based on volume forecast. My manager asked me to release six casuals. I looked at the forecast, it was showing lower volume for Thursday and Friday. What I checked was only whether the forecast is the latest version, that is all, and it was updated that morning. So I released four instead of six, keeping two as buffer. Friday the volume came almost 20 per cent more than forecast because two customers advanced their orders, and we ran late by two hours. But since the decision was as per the plan sheet nobody said anything to me about it.
Q3_text: Sir honestly there is no way to tell. The WMS shows live data, that is what we have been told, so we take it as live. Sometimes the scanner data comes late and then the numbers correct themselves after an hour, we all know this, so if a number looks strange we simply wait and refresh. No warning message comes. Nothing like that in our system. Only when the whole screen does not load, then we know it is down.
Q4_text: Yes one time the inventory accuracy report was showing 99.2 per cent for our warehouse which was not possible because we had just had a big mismatch in the cycle count of one aisle. When I checked, the report was picking last month's audit and not the current one. But I did not do much about it because that report goes to head office and it was showing us in good light, so nobody was going to complain about it, including me. That is the truth.
Q5_text: Nothing happened after that because I did not raise it formally. I mentioned it to my manager casually and he said leave it, it will correct next month. Which it did. There is no place where I can write such a thing. We do not have any such system. If I send a mail then it becomes a big issue and people start asking why are you highlighting, so mostly we discuss in person only.
Q6_text: Report is much easier to defend, one hundred per cent. If I take a decision on my own thinking and it goes wrong, then the question is why did you do like that. If the same thing goes wrong and I show the plan sheet, then it is a planning problem, not my problem. Everybody in operations knows this. That is why we always keep the mail and the screenshot.
Q7_text: Very different. If I follow the system and it fails, at most there is a discussion in the morning meeting and it is over. If I go against the system and it fails, then it comes in my review and my manager will say you should have escalated instead of deciding yourself. Actually even if it goes right, going against the system is risky because next time also they will expect you to take the risk. So the safe thing is to follow and inform.
Q8_text: Our loaders and the supervisor at the dock keep saying that the system is showing loads as departed when actually the vehicle is standing in the yard waiting for documents. They say it daily. It is not written anywhere. It gets discussed in the shift handover and then forgotten. Once our supervisor took photos of the vehicles standing and sent on WhatsApp group, that was the only time some action happened and a person was deputed for documents. But no formal record.
Q9_text: Yes because whatever the sheet shows, that only we discuss. Manpower, overtime, vehicle count. Option which never comes is talking to the customer for changing the delivery window, because that is sales team's matter and we do not have any data for it. Also we never discuss reducing the number of SKUs picked per wave, because the wave planning is automatic.
Q10_prompt: In the study you have just completed, in the scenario about renewing a supplier at increased volume the dashboard indicated that the supplier scored 98.6 per cent and should be renewed at higher volume, while what you knew locally was that the inspector had been passing batches by eye because the test rig was out of calibration. You chose: Renew at increased volume, as the scorecard recommends.Looking back, what would drive your choice if this were a real decision at your work?
Q10_text: I chose to renew as per the scorecard. If I am honest that is what I would do at my work also, and not because I think the score is right. The scorecard is prepared by the central team and if I say hold, then I have to prove why, and I do not have any test report to show. The inspector telling me something verbally is not evidence I can put in a mail. If I hold the renewal and production stops for want of material, that is directly on me. If I renew and there is a quality problem after six months, it will be a supplier issue and a quality issue, my name will not come. So the real thing driving it is who has to answer. I know it is not the correct answer for the company but that is how it works.
Q11_text: If the system itself shows that this data is old or this test is pending, then it becomes easy. Then I can simply forward that screen to my manager and say the system itself is saying it. Right now if I want to raise something I have to say it in my own words, and my words are not evidence. Give me the evidence on the screen and I will raise it every time.
Q12_text: No, nothing further. Good survey, the situations were quite realistic actually.

Q1_text: I use the WMS dashboard and one daily dispatch tracker in Google Sheets which our MIS boy updates. WMS one I keep open the whole day on the second monitor. First thing I check is pending picklist count and the dock utilisation, because that decides whether I have to call for extra manpower or not. Also there is one SLA screen showing on time dispatch percentage which my reporting manager sees, so I check that before he checks it.
Q2_text: Two weeks back the manpower planning sheet showed that the evening shift was overstaffed by six people based on volume forecast. My manager asked me to release six casuals. I looked at the forecast, it was showing lower volume for Thursday and Friday. What I checked was only whether the forecast is the latest version, that is all, and it was updated that morning. So I released four instead of six, keeping two as buffer. Friday the volume came almost 20 per cent more than forecast because two customers advanced their orders, and we ran late by two hours. But since the decision was as per the plan sheet nobody said anything to me about it.
Q3_text: Sir honestly there is no way to tell. The WMS shows live data, that is what we have been told, so we take it as live. Sometimes the scanner data comes late and then the numbers correct themselves after an hour, we all know this, so if a number looks strange we simply wait and refresh. No warning message comes. Nothing like that in our system. Only when the whole screen does not load, then we know it is down.
Q4_text: Yes one time the inventory accuracy report was showing 99.2 per cent for our warehouse which was not possible because we had just had a big mismatch in the cycle count of one aisle. When I checked, the report was picking last month's audit and not the current one. But I did not do much about it because that report goes to head office and it was showing us in good light, so nobody was going to complain about it, including me. That is the truth.
Q5_text: Nothing happened after that because I did not raise it formally. I mentioned it to my manager casually and he said leave it, it will correct next month. Which it did. There is no place where I can write such a thing. We do not have any such system. If I send a mail then it becomes a big issue and people start asking why are you highlighting, so mostly we discuss in person only.
Q6_text: Report is much easier to defend, one hundred per cent. If I take a decision on my own thinking and it goes wrong, then the question is why did you do like that. If the same thing goes wrong and I show the plan sheet, then it is a planning problem, not my problem. Everybody in operations knows this. That is why we always keep the mail and the screenshot.
Q7_text: Very different. If I follow the system and it fails, at most there is a discussion in the morning meeting and it is over. If I go against the system and it fails, then it comes in my review and my manager will say you should have escalated instead of deciding yourself. Actually even if it goes right, going against the system is risky because next time also they will expect you to take the risk. So the safe thing is to follow and inform.
Q8_text: Our loaders and the supervisor at the dock keep saying that the system is showing loads as departed when actually the vehicle is standing in the yard waiting for documents. They say it daily. It is not written anywhere. It gets discussed in the shift handover and then forgotten. Once our supervisor took photos of the vehicles standing and sent on WhatsApp group, that was the only time some action happened and a person was deputed for documents. But no formal record.
Q9_text: Yes because whatever the sheet shows, that only we discuss. Manpower, overtime, vehicle count. Option which never comes is talking to the customer for changing the delivery window, because that is sales team's matter and we do not have any data for it. Also we never discuss reducing the number of SKUs picked per wave, because the wave planning is automatic.
Q10_prompt: In the study you have just completed, in the scenario about renewing a supplier at increased volume the dashboard indicated that the supplier scored 98.6 per cent and should be renewed at higher volume, while what you knew locally was that the inspector had been passing batches by eye because the test rig was out of calibration. You chose: Renew at increased volume, as the scorecard recommends.Looking back, what would drive your choice if this were a real decision at your work?
Q10_text: I chose to renew as per the scorecard. If I am honest that is what I would do at my work also, and not because I think the score is right. The scorecard is prepared by the central team and if I say hold, then I have to prove why, and I do not have any test report to show. The inspector telling me something verbally is not evidence I can put in a mail. If I hold the renewal and production stops for want of material, that is directly on me. If I renew and there is a quality problem after six months, it will be a supplier issue and a quality issue, my name will not come. So the real thing driving it is who has to answer. I know it is not the correct answer for the company but that is how it works.
Q11_text: If the system itself shows that this data is old or this test is pending, then it becomes easy. Then I can simply forward that screen to my manager and say the system itself is saying it. Right now if I want to raise something I have to say it in my own words, and my words are not evidence. Give me the evidence on the screen and I will raise it every time.
Q12_text: No, nothing further. Good survey, the situations were quite realistic actually.
